mathprize-2011-01.title: Parametrize the solutions
mathprize-2011-01.body:
One solution is $(m,n)=(0,25)$, and all solutions are $(4t,\,25-3t)$ for integer $t$. Then $m-n=7t-25$. The multiples-of-7 shift gives values $\dots,-4,3,10,\dots$ (for $t=3,4,5$), so the smallest absolute value is $3$ (at $t=4$, $(m,n)=(16,13)$).

**Answer: 3**

mathprize-2011-02.title: Square the guess
mathprize-2011-02.body:
Try $\frac{1+\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$: its square is $\frac{4+2\sqrt3}{2}=2+\sqrt3$, and it is positive. So $a=1$, $b=3$, $c=2$ and $\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}=\frac{1+\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$.

(Equivalently, $\sqrt{2+\sqrt3}=\sqrt{\frac{4+2\sqrt3}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{(1+\sqrt3)^2}}{\sqrt2}$.)

**Answer: $\frac{1+\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$**

mathprize-2011-03.title: Lunes of Hippocrates
mathprize-2011-03.body:
$20^2+21^2=400+441=841=29^2$, so the angle at $A$ is a right angle and the semicircle on $BC$ passes through $A$. Each shaded crescent is a small semicircle minus the circular segment cut off by chord $AB$ or $AC$. The semicircle on $BC$ equals the triangle plus those two segments. So shaded = (two small semicircles) - (semicircle on $BC$ - triangle). By the Pythagorean theorem the two small semicircles together have the area of the big one, so the shaded area equals the area of the triangle: $\frac12\cdot20\cdot21=210$.

**Answer: 210**

mathprize-2011-04.title: Rewrite both terms as powers of 10
mathprize-2011-04.body:
Let $u=\log\log x$ and $w=\log\log\log x$ (both defined since $x>10$ gives $\log x>1$ and $u>0$). Then $\log x=10^{u}$, so the first term is $(10^{u})^{w}=10^{uw}$.

For the second term, $u=10^{w}$, so $u^{u}=(10^{w})^{u}=10^{uw}$.

The two terms are equal, so the difference is always $0$.

**Answer: 0**

mathprize-2011-05.title: Inradius and tangent lengths
mathprize-2011-05.body:
The triangle is right-angled at $B$. The inradius is $r=\frac{3+4-5}2=1$. The tangent lengths from the vertices are $s-a$: from $A$: $s-BC=6-4=2$; from $B$: $s-AC=1$; from $C$: $s-AB=3$. Then $AI=\sqrt{2^2+1^2}=\sqrt5$, $BI=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2$, $CI=\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}$. The product is $\sqrt{5\cdot2\cdot10}=10$.

**Answer: 10**

mathprize-2011-06.title: Place the circles in opposite corners
mathprize-2011-06.body:
Put the circles in opposite corners of the square, tangent to each other. Their centers are at distance $2$ and lie on a diagonal, so each center is $1$ from two sides and the horizontal gap between the centers is $\sqrt2$. Hence the side is $1+\sqrt2+1=2+\sqrt2$ and the area is $(2+\sqrt2)^2=6+4\sqrt2$. (The centers must be at distance $\ge2$ and each at least $1$ from every side, so a smaller square is impossible: the centers lie in a square of side $s-2$ and must be at distance $\ge2$ so the diagonal of that square is at least $2$, giving $s-2\ge\sqrt2$.)

**Answer: $6+4\sqrt2$**

mathprize-2011-07.title: Use the recurrence
mathprize-2011-07.body:
Let $s_n=z^n+z^{-n}$; then $s_{n+1}=\sqrt3\,s_n-s_{n-1}$ with $s_0=2$, $s_1=\sqrt3$. This gives $2,\sqrt3,1,0,-1,-\sqrt3,-2,-\sqrt3,-1,0,1,\sqrt3,2,\dots$, with period $12$. Since $2010=12\cdot167+6$, $s_{2010}=s_6=-2$.

**Answer: $-2$**

mathprize-2011-08.title: Disk minus shadow plus two sectors
mathprize-2011-08.body:
Points reached by straight segments from $A$: the disk of radius $8$ around $A$ minus the "shadow" of $\overline{BC}$. The shadow is the part of the $60^\circ$ sector at $A$ (bounded by rays $AB$, $AC$) beyond $BC$: sector area $\frac16\pi\cdot8^2=\frac{32\pi}3$ minus the equilateral triangle $ABC$ of area $9\sqrt3$. 

Points in the shadow's complement behind $BC$ reached by bending around $B$ or $C$: after walking $6$ to $B$ there is $2$ left, so we gain a sector of radius $2$ at $B$ and one at $C$. Each sector is bounded by the ray $BC$ and the extension of $AB$ beyond $B$, an angle of $120^\circ$, with area $\frac13\pi\cdot4=\frac{4\pi}3$ (these sectors are disjoint).

Total: $64\pi-\left(\frac{32\pi}3-9\sqrt3\right)+\frac{8\pi}3=56\pi+9\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $56\pi+9\sqrt3$**

mathprize-2011-09.title: Barycentric coordinates
mathprize-2011-09.body:
Write points as combinations of $A,B,C$. $D=\frac12B+\frac12C$; $E=\frac12A+\frac14B+\frac14C$; $F=\frac12B+\frac12E=\frac14A+\frac58B+\frac18C$. So $F=\frac78G'+\frac18C$ where $G'=\frac27A+\frac57B$ lies on $AB$. Thus $G'$ is on line $CF$ and on $AB$, i.e. $G'=G$, and $AG=\frac57AB$.

**Answer: $\frac57$**

mathprize-2011-09.title: Coordinates
mathprize-2011-09.body:
Take $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(0,1)$. Then $D=(\frac12,\frac12)$, $E=(\frac14,\frac14)$, $F=(\frac58,\frac18)$. Line $CF$: from $(0,1)$ with direction $(\frac58,-\frac78)$ meets $y=0$ at $t=\frac87$, $x=\frac58\cdot\frac87=\frac57$. So $AG/AB=\frac57$.

**Answer: $\frac57$**

mathprize-2011-10.title: Take tangents
mathprize-2011-10.body:
Move the first term: $\tan^{-1}(ax)+\tan^{-1}(bx)=\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac1x-\frac x8\right)$. Taking tangents, the right side gives $\dfrac1{\frac1x-\frac x8}=\dfrac{x}{1-\frac{x^2}8}$ and the left side gives $\dfrac{(a+b)x}{1-abx^2}$. These agree for all $x$ exactly when $a+b=1$ and $ab=\frac18$. Then $a^2+b^2=(a+b)^2-2ab=1-\frac14=\frac34$.

**Answer: $\frac34$**

mathprize-2011-12.title: S moves the first digit to the end
mathprize-2011-12.body:
$10^{\lfloor\log n\rfloor}$ is the largest power of ten at most $n$, so the first term is the leading digit $a$ of $n$ and the bracket is the remaining digits; $S$ removes the leading digit, multiplies the rest by 10, and adds the digit: a cyclic rotation $abc\ldots\mapsto bc\ldots a$ (if the second digit is $0$, the result has fewer digits and the next application of $S$ no longer restores $n$).

- 1 digit: $S(n)=n$: $9$ numbers.
- 2 digits $ab$: $S(S(ab))=ab$ when $b\ne0$: $9\cdot9=81$.
- 3 digits $abc$: need $b\ne0$ and $abc=cab$, so $a=b=c$: $9$.
- 4 digits $abcd\le2011$: need $b\ne0$ and $abcd=cdab$, so $a=c$, $b=d$; with $n\le2011$, $a=c=1$, $b$ any nonzero digit: $9$.

Total $9+81+9+9=108$.

**Answer: 108**

mathprize-2011-14.title: $F$ is linear in $q$
mathprize-2011-14.body:
Expanding, $F(p,q)=(7-12p)q+(7p-4)$. A linear function of $q$ on $[0,1]$ is maximized at an endpoint: $G(p)=\max(F(p,0),F(p,1))=\max(7p-4,\,3-5p)$. The first is increasing and the second decreasing in $p$, so $G$ is smallest where they are equal: $7p-4=3-5p$, $p=\frac7{12}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{12}$**

mathprize-2011-15.title: Reduce the condition
mathprize-2011-15.body:
Clearing denominators, $\frac{a+b}{c+d}=\frac12\left(\frac ac+\frac bd\right)$ becomes $2(a+b)cd=(ad+bc)(c+d)$, i.e. $acd+bcd-ad^2-bc^2=0$, i.e. $ad(c-d)-bc(c-d)=0$, i.e. $(c-d)(ad-bc)=0$. So either $c=d$ or $ad=bc$.

- $c=d$: probability $\frac16$, i.e. $216$ of the $1296$ outcomes.
- $ad=bc$, i.e. $a/b=c/d$. With $a=2^i,b=2^j,c=2^k,d=2^l$ this means $i+l=j+k$. The number of solutions is $\sum_sN(s)^2$ where $N(s)$ counts pairs from $\{1,\dots,6\}$ with sum $s$: $1+4+9+16+25+36+25+16+9+4+1=146$.
- Both $c=d$ and $ad=bc$ force $a=b$: $6\cdot6=36$ outcomes.

Total $\frac{216+146-36}{1296}=\frac{326}{1296}=\frac{163}{648}$.

**Answer: $\frac{163}{648}$**

mathprize-2011-16.title: Area of the ellipse
mathprize-2011-16.body:
$N$ is the number of lattice points in the ellipse $4x^2+9y^2\le10^9$, which has semi-axes $\frac{\sqrt{10^9}}2$ and $\frac{\sqrt{10^9}}3$ and area $\pi\cdot\frac{10^9}{6}\approx523{,}598{,}776$. Placing a unit square at each lattice point, the union of the squares has area $N$ and differs from the ellipse area by an amount of the order of the perimeter ($\sim10^5$). So $N$ lies strictly between $5.2\times10^8$ and $5.3\times10^8$, and $a=5$, $b=2$. (A direct count gives $N=523{,}598{,}683$.)

**Answer: 52**

mathprize-2011-17.title: Split into three multiples of $x^2+x+1$
mathprize-2011-17.body:
Write $x^{512}+x^{256}+1=(x^{512}+x^{511}+\dots+1)-(x^{511}+\dots+x^{257})-(x^{255}+\dots+x)$. Each bracket is a geometric sum whose number of terms is divisible by $3$ ($513$, $255$ and $255$ terms), so each is a multiple of $x^2+x+1$:

$x^{512}+\dots+1=(x^2+x+1)(x^{510}+x^{507}+\dots+1)$ ($171$ terms),
$x^{511}+\dots+x^{257}=(x^2+x+1)(x^{509}+\dots+x^{257})$ ($85$ terms),
$x^{255}+\dots+x=(x^2+x+1)(x^{253}+\dots+x)$ ($85$ terms).

So $P$ is the first quotient minus the other two, and the three sets of exponents are disjoint (they are $\equiv0$, $\equiv2$ and $\equiv1\pmod3$ respectively). The number of nonzero coefficients is $171+85+85=341$.

**Answer: 341**

mathprize-2011-18.title: Constant term and $P(c)$
mathprize-2011-18.body:
Write $P(x)=ax^2+bx+c$. Since $P(n)\equiv c\pmod n$, $\gcd(c,n)=1$ for every $n$, so $c=\pm1$. Then $P(P(n))\equiv P(c)\pmod n$, so likewise $P(c)=\pm1$. If $c=1$: $9a+3b+1=89$ has no solution (not divisible by $3$). So $c=-1$ and $3a+b=30$. Then $P(-1)=a-b-1=\pm1$ gives $a-b=2$ or $0$; with $b=30-3a$ this gives $4a=32$, $a=8$, $b=6$ (the other case $4a=30$ is impossible). So $P(x)=8x^2+6x-1$ (and indeed $P(-1)=1$), and $P(10)=800+60-1=859$.

**Answer: 859**

mathprize-2011-19.title: Multiplicative structure
mathprize-2011-19.body:
Let $f(t)=\frac{t-1}{t+1}$ for $t>0$. A computation gives $f(b)\oplus f(c)=\frac{(b-1)(c+1)+(b+1)(c-1)}{(b+1)(c+1)+(b-1)(c-1)}=\frac{2bc-2}{2bc+2}=f(bc)$. So $\oplus$ corresponds to multiplication of the arguments. Fourteen copies of $v=f(17^{1/7})$ give $f\left(17^{14/7}\right)=f(289)=\frac{288}{290}=\frac{144}{145}$.

**Answer: $\frac{144}{145}$**

mathprize-2011-20.title: Area of an ellipse sector
mathprize-2011-20.body:
Let $x=AX$, $y=AY$. By the Law of Cosines $XY^2=x^2+y^2-xy$. The condition is $x^2+y^2-xy\le\frac1{\sqrt3}$ for $(x,y)\in[0,1]^2$. This is an ellipse; since $XY\le3^{-1/4}<\frac{\sqrt3}2$... the ellipse does not reach the lines $x=1$ or $y=1$ (at those the minimum of $XY$ is $\frac{\sqrt3}2>3^{-1/4}$), so $p$ is the area of the part of the ellipse in the first quadrant. In coordinates rotated by $45^\circ$ the ellipse is $u^2+3v^2\le\frac2{\sqrt3}$ and the axes become the lines $v=\pm u$. Stretching $v$ by $\sqrt3$ gives a circle $u^2+v^2\le\frac2{\sqrt3}$ and the lines become $v=\pm\sqrt3u$, an angle of $120^\circ$ (one third of the circle). The sector area is $\frac13\pi\cdot\frac2{\sqrt3}=\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3}$; undoing the stretch divides by $\sqrt3$, so $p=\frac{2\pi}9$. Hence $900p=200\pi\approx628.3$, which rounds to $628$.

**Answer: 628**
